findings.claim: Financial accounting, by definition, exists to communicate financial information to stakeholders outside the organisation — owners, stockholders, lenders, regulators (SEC, IRS), customers, employees, and the public.
findings.failure_mode: definition's list widened; employees placed outside the organisation
findings.evidence: Deep 25 [V]: financial accounting is 'used to generate information for stakeholders outside of an organization, such as owners, stockholders, lenders, and governmental entities such as the SEC and the IRS'. Managers and employees are internal (deep 43; managerial accounting serves them, deep 25).
findings.fix: correct: Financial accounting, by definition, generates information for stakeholders outside the organisation — owners, stockholders, lenders, and governmental entities such as the SEC and IRS (Ch 1.1); Ch 1.4 widens the stakeholder set to customers and employees.

findings.claim: Ch 1.4 ("Explain Why Accounting Is Important to Business Stakeholders" [V])
findings.failure_mode: marker on a section title
findings.evidence: A section heading is a citation locator, not a quoted claim; the corpus convention (commit 572b1ba) is that section titles in citations carry no [V].
findings.fix: re-mark: drop [V] from the section title

findings.claim: naming six categories (stockholders, creditors and lenders, governmental and regulatory agencies, customers, managers and employees, plus implicit communities and suppliers)

findings.claim: Stakeholder-engagement decisions are then threaded through every subsequent chapter.

findings.claim: the Dodge v. Ford "business judgment rule" that explicitly extends managerial fiduciary duty beyond pure shareholder primacy

notes: Faithful core: the long [V] quotations are verbatim (Ch 2.1 utilitarian box, source 3783-3789; tone at the top, source 22323-22327; the Dodge v. Ford stakeholder passage, source 36643-36656; stakeholder definition, source 1771-1773), the five categories and their interests, three sources of capital, SOX 302/404, audit committee and auditor independence, the Ch 8.7 fraud taxonomy, and the COSO components. Integration rows for Business Ethics (CSR, triple bottom line, moral minimum, stakeholder pluralism), Accounting Vol 2 and the Mintzberg liaison role check out. Drift clusters in three places: consequence claims about trust and penalties that no source passage carries (restatement preserving trust, late disclosure compounding penalty, cover-up costs), a whistleblower/Watkins thread borrowed from the Business Ethics source without attribution, and marker handling (a [V] court quotation that should be [BT], unmarked or non-verbatim quotations at lines 22, 30, 36, and a continuity note that invents an [AE] marker). Source-supported gaps worth cycling to the deep: the consistency principle (Ch 10.1) and restatement (Ch 14.4).
